description: Every other control depends on leadership and staff showing a real commitment to honest and ethical conduct. A documented, acknowledged code of conduct is the artifact auditors look for as evidence that expectations were set and accepted rather than assumed.
implementation_guidance:
Publish a code of conduct covering ethical behaviour, acceptable use, conflicts of interest and confidentiality.
Require every employee and contractor to acknowledge it at hire and annually thereafter.
Track acknowledgement centrally so completion can be evidenced per person.
Route non-completion through the disciplinary process rather than leaving it open.
name: Code of conduct and ethics policy

evidence.name: Approved code of conduct
evidence.what: Approved code of conduct
evidence.where: Written in the Documents module from the code of conduct template and approved by the CEO or a founder.
evidence.shows: Ethics, acceptable use, conflicts of interest, confidentiality, what happens on a breach, owner, approval date and next review date.

evidence.name: Acknowledgement from every member of staff
evidence.what: Signed acknowledgement of the code from each person
evidence.where: Sent from the Documents module as an acknowledgement campaign at hire and once a year.
evidence.shows: One acknowledgement per employee and contractor, with name and date, covering everyone on the staff list for the period.

evidence.name: Record of breaches and the action taken
evidence.what: Log of code of conduct breaches and the action taken
evidence.where: A private sheet or HR tool note kept by the CEO or HR lead, with the case notes filed against each entry.
evidence.shows: Date raised, what happened, who decided, the action taken and the date closed.
evidence.if_none: A dated note from the HR lead or CEO: "no code of conduct breaches in [period]".

description: People must know there are consequences when they disregard their security responsibilities, or those responsibilities carry no weight. A documented and consistently applied disciplinary process is what makes policy enforceable rather than advisory.
implementation_guidance:
Define the disciplinary process in policy, including the range of sanctions and who decides them.
Reference it in the code of conduct that staff acknowledge, so the consequence is known in advance.
Apply it consistently when violations occur, as inconsistent enforcement undermines the control.
Retain records of the decision and its basis, handled confidentially through HR.
name: Documented disciplinary process

evidence.name: Disciplinary procedure
evidence.what: Disciplinary procedure
evidence.where: Usually a section of the employee handbook, kept in the Documents module and approved by the CEO.
evidence.shows: Steps from warning to dismissal, who decides, how security breaches are handled, the right to respond, and how records are kept.

evidence.name: List of all disciplinary cases in the period, with date opened, issue, steps taken, outcome and date closed. The auditor chooses the sample from it.
evidence.what: List of disciplinary cases in the period
evidence.where: Kept by HR or the founder who handles people matters, in the HR tool or a private sheet.
evidence.shows: Every case opened in the period with date, the rule broken, the steps of the procedure followed, the outcome and the date closed.
evidence.if_none: A dated note from the HR lead: "no disciplinary cases in [period]".

description: Security duties are only as effective as the reporting lines and authorities behind them, so both must be established. An accurate structure shows that security duties sit with real roles holding the standing to carry them out, rather than being distributed informally.
implementation_guidance:
Maintain a current organizational chart showing reporting lines.
Maintain role descriptions that state the security responsibilities attached to each role.
Review both at least annually and after any reorganization.
Confirm security roles retain a reporting line independent enough to raise issues without conflict of interest.
name: Organizational structure and reporting lines

evidence.name: Current organization chart with reporting lines
evidence.what: Organization chart with reporting lines
evidence.where: Exported from the HR tool such as Rippling, Gusto or BambooHR, or a slide kept by the CEO.
evidence.shows: Every person or role, who they report to, the security owner, and the date the chart was current.

evidence.name: Role descriptions for security and compliance roles
evidence.what: Role descriptions for security and compliance roles
evidence.where: A short document per role, kept with the job descriptions in the HR tool or shared drive.
evidence.shows: For the security lead, control owners and anyone with compliance duties: purpose, duties, authority and who they report to.

evidence.name: Minutes where the board or leadership reviewed the structure
evidence.what: Leadership minutes reviewing the org structure
evidence.where: Notes from a leadership or board meeting, kept in the shared drive or meeting notes tool.
evidence.shows: Date, who attended, that the structure and reporting lines were reviewed, the changes agreed and who owns them.

description: A security programme without a single accountable owner fragments across teams and stalls at decisions nobody is empowered to make. A formally designated officer gives the programme an escalation point and gives the auditor a name.
implementation_guidance:
Formally designate a security officer or equivalent lead in policy or by board resolution.
Document the role's authority, budget and escalation path, and its reporting line to the oversight body, and where a regulator requires it, keep the role independent of IT operations, for example reporting to the chief executive or the chief risk officer.
Name a deputy so accountability survives absence and turnover.
Review the designation whenever the role changes hands.
name: Designated security officer

evidence.name: Appointment or role charter naming the security officer
evidence.what: Appointment letter or role charter for the security officer
evidence.where: An email or short memo from the CEO, or a signed role charter in the shared drive.
evidence.shows: Name of the security officer, start date, duties, authority, and that they report to leadership.

evidence.name: Report or briefing from the security officer to leadership
evidence.what: Quarterly security briefing to leadership
evidence.where: Slides or a written update shared at a leadership meeting, filed with the meeting notes.
evidence.shows: Date, audience, status of risks, incidents, audit findings and open actions, and any decisions asked for.

description: A governing body independent of management is what holds the security program to account, rather than leaving management to judge its own work. Without a documented record of that oversight there is no evidence that leadership exercised the accountability it carries.
implementation_guidance:
Put security posture, material incidents, risk assessment results and remediation progress on the board or oversight-body agenda at least annually, and quarterly where practical.
Provide a written pack rather than a verbal update, so the information given to the body is itself evidence.
Retain agendas, packs and minutes recording what was discussed and decided.
Record any resourcing or risk-acceptance decisions the body makes.
name: Board / executive security oversight

evidence.name: Charter of the board or executive committee covering security oversight
evidence.what: Terms of reference for security oversight
evidence.where: A board resolution or a one page terms of reference for the leadership team, kept in the shared drive.
evidence.shows: Which body oversees security, how often it meets, what it reviews, who sits on it, and the approval date.

evidence.name: Minutes showing security was discussed and challenged
evidence.what: Board or leadership minutes with a security item
evidence.where: Minutes from the board or leadership meeting each quarter, kept in the shared drive.
evidence.shows: Date, attendees, the security topics covered, questions asked, decisions made and follow up actions.

evidence.name: Record of who sits on the body and their independence
evidence.what: List of members of the oversight body
evidence.where: The board register, or a short list kept with the terms of reference.
evidence.shows: Each member's name, role, start date, and whether they are independent of day to day management.

description: Monitoring only closes the loop when results reach people who can allocate resources. A recurring management review is where control health, findings and risk are considered together, and where remediation is prioritized against everything else competing for effort.
implementation_guidance:
Hold a management review at least quarterly, attended by the security lead and by senior managers who can commit resources, covering control health, open findings, incidents, risk register changes and remediation progress.
At least once a year, have the executive team review whether the security program still fits the business, covers what it needs to and works, using actions from earlier reviews, changes in internal and external factors and in what interested parties require, nonconformities and corrective actions, measurement and audit results, objectives achieved, feedback from customers and others, risk assessment results and treatment status, and ideas for improvement.
Record attendees, the inputs considered, decisions on improvements and on any changes the program needs, resource commitments and actions with named owners, and carry unresolved actions forward rather than closing them silently.
Escalate items that have missed two consecutive reviews to the oversight body.
name: Periodic management review of security

evidence.name: Management review agenda and minutes
evidence.what: Management review minutes
evidence.where: Notes from the quarterly leadership meeting where security is reviewed, uploaded after each meeting.
evidence.shows: Date, attendees, inputs covered such as audit results, incidents, risks and objectives, decisions made and actions with owners.

evidence.name: Actions raised in the review and their closure
evidence.what: Management review actions tracked to closure
evidence.where: Tasks module, one task per action raised in the review.
evidence.shows: Each action with owner, due date, status and closure date, and a note on any that slipped.
evidence.if_none: The review minutes stating that no actions were raised.

description: Accountability that is not assigned is not accountability. Authorities and responsibilities must be defined so individuals know what they own, and so a failing control has a name attached to it.
implementation_guidance:
Map every control to a named owner, and record the authority that owner holds to act.
Review the mapping at least annually and whenever someone changes role or leaves.
Reassign ownership as part of offboarding so no control is left orphaned.
Keep ownership at the level of a person, not a team inbox, for controls that require judgement.
name: Assigned control ownership (RACI)

evidence.name: Control ownership register
evidence.what: Control ownership register
evidence.where: The Controls module, where each control has a named owner.
evidence.shows: Every control in scope with one owner who is a current member of staff.

evidence.name: Updated ownership when roles change
evidence.what: Owner changes made after a leaver or role change
evidence.where: The Controls module history when an owner is changed.
evidence.shows: Date of change, control, old owner, new owner, and the reason, such as a leaver.
evidence.if_none: A dated note from the security lead that no control owner left or changed role in [period].

description: Risks can only be identified against objectives that have been stated. The system description defines the boundary, the commitments made to customers and the requirements that follow, and it anchors both the risk assessment and the audit scope.
implementation_guidance:
Document the system boundary, covering infrastructure, software, people, procedures and data.
State the commitments made to customers and the legal, regulatory, contractual and internal requirements the system must meet, as those are what the controls are designed and audited against.
Describe the third parties the system depends on, and state clearly which controls they operate and which remain yours.
Review annually and on material change, and reconcile the description against what is actually deployed.
name: System description and service commitments

evidence.name: System description covering boundary, services, infrastructure, people and data
evidence.what: System description
evidence.where: A document written by the CTO or a founder, usually in the shared drive, and reused in the audit report.
evidence.shows: Services offered, system boundary, infrastructure, software, people, data, third parties and key controls, current for the period.

evidence.name: Customer commitments and the requirements the system must meet
evidence.what: List of customer commitments and the system requirements behind them
evidence.where: Taken from the terms of service, standard contract, SLA and security page, summarized in one document.
evidence.shows: Each promise made to customers, such as uptime, encryption and breach notice, and the system requirement that meets it.

description: The risk assessment is the foundation the rest of the programme rests on: it determines which controls are needed and where effort is justified. Controls selected without one are difficult to defend as sufficient.
implementation_guidance:
Perform a formal risk assessment at least annually, and on significant change to the business or environment, taking account of internal and external factors and the requirements of customers, regulators and other parties.
Identify risks to the confidentiality, integrity and availability of information in scope, to the commitments made to customers and to the security program meeting its objectives, including fraud and third-party risk, and name an owner for each.
Score likelihood and impact against a documented scale, record inherent and residual risk, compare each result with acceptance criteria approved by leadership that state what level of risk may be accepted and by whom, and rank risks for treatment.
Retain the methodology and results so assessments are reproducible and comparable year over year, and where a standard or contract leaves the frequency of a control to you, keep a short risk analysis that justifies the frequency chosen and review it yearly.
name: Annual risk assessment

evidence.name: Risk assessment report with method and scope
evidence.what: Annual risk assessment report
evidence.where: The Risks module, run once a year using the written risk method, with the report exported.
evidence.shows: Date, scope, method, each risk with likelihood, impact and score, who took part, and the treatment chosen.

evidence.name: Management sign off on the assessment
evidence.what: Leadership sign off on the risk assessment
evidence.where: A signed memo, email or meeting minute from the CEO approving the assessment.
evidence.shows: Date, who approved, which assessment version, and acceptance of the remaining risk levels.

description: A risk that is identified but not tracked is not managed. The register is the operational record showing each risk has an owner, a rating and a decision, and it is what an auditor traces from assessment through to control.
implementation_guidance:
Capture risk description, category, owner, inherent rating, mitigating controls, residual rating and treatment decision of accept, mitigate, transfer or avoid.
Review the register at each management review and record rating changes with dates.
Require named sign-off at an appropriate level for any accepted risk.
Link each risk to the controls that mitigate it so coverage can be verified.
name: Risk register with treatment decisions

evidence.name: Risk register with owners, ratings and treatment decisions
evidence.what: Risk register
evidence.where: The Risks module register, kept current through the year.
evidence.shows: Each risk with owner, likelihood, impact, score, treatment decision and date of last review.

evidence.name: Approval of each accepted risk
evidence.what: Approval record for each accepted risk
evidence.where: The acceptance step in the Risks module, approved by someone other than the person asking.
evidence.shows: Risk, reason for acceptance, who approved, date, and the expiry or next review date.
evidence.if_none: A dated note from the risk owner that no risks were accepted in [period].

description: A treatment decision only reduces risk once it is executed. The treatment plan turns intent into scheduled, owned work, and it is the evidence that residual risk ratings reflect reality rather than aspiration.
implementation_guidance:
For each risk being mitigated, record the specific treatment actions, the accountable owner, the target date and the expected residual rating, and have the risk owner approve the plan.
Track actions to closure with evidence rather than status updates alone.
Re-rate the risk only once the treatment is demonstrably in place, and have the risk owner accept the remaining risk in writing, or send it back for further treatment where it is above the acceptance criteria. When someone other than the risk owner requests the acceptance, name the risk owner as its approver.
Report overdue treatment actions at management review.
name: Risk treatment plan

evidence.name: Treatment plan with owners and due dates
evidence.what: Risk treatment plan
evidence.where: The Risks module, where each treated risk lists its planned actions.
evidence.shows: Each action with its risk, owner, due date and status.

evidence.name: Completed risk treatment tasks with proof of each change
evidence.what: Closed treatment tasks with proof of each change
evidence.where: Tasks module, one task per treatment action, closed with a screenshot, ticket or setting change attached.
evidence.shows: Action, owner, date closed, the proof of the change, and the risk it reduced.
evidence.if_none: A dated note that no treatment actions fell due in [period], with the plan showing the due dates.

evidence.name: Risk owner acceptance of the remaining risk after treatment
evidence.what: Risk owner acceptance of the remaining risk
evidence.where: The acceptance step on each risk in the Risks module once treatment is done.
evidence.shows: Risk, remaining score, risk owner, and date accepted.
evidence.if_none: A dated note that no treatment was finished in [period].

evidence.name: Risk owner approval of each treatment plan
evidence.what: Risk owner approval of each treatment plan
evidence.where: An email, ticket comment or signed note from the risk owner, uploaded against the plan.
evidence.shows: Risk, the plan approved, owner name, date, and the remaining risk level the owner expects to accept.
evidence.if_none: A dated note that no new treatment plans were made in [period].

description: Fraud risk, including insider misuse and management override, must be considered explicitly in the risk assessment, because the people with legitimate access are the ones best placed to abuse it. Teams routinely assess external threats and omit this, which is a recurring exception.
implementation_guidance:
Include a fraud and insider-threat section in the annual risk assessment, covering incentive, opportunity and rationalization.
Consider management override of controls specifically, as it is the scenario most often left out.
Map identified fraud risks to mitigations such as least privilege, segregation of duties, logging and independent review.
Record the conclusion even where the assessed risk is low.
name: Fraud and insider-threat consideration

evidence.name: Fraud risk assessment covering insider misuse and management override
evidence.what: Fraud and insider misuse risks in the risk assessment
evidence.where: Risks module, as a set of fraud risks added during the annual risk assessment.
evidence.shows: Risks such as payment fraud, data theft by staff, and leaders overriding controls, each with a score and a treatment.

evidence.name: Actions taken on the fraud risks found
evidence.what: Actions taken on fraud risks
evidence.where: Tickets or tasks closed for each fraud risk, with proof attached, such as the two person payment approval setting.
evidence.shows: Each fraud risk, the action taken, owner, date, and proof that the change is live.
evidence.if_none: The assessment showing every fraud risk was accepted, with the approval.

description: Risk assessed once a year goes stale as soon as the environment changes. A new subprocessor, a new data type or a major architectural shift can introduce risk that the annual cycle will not surface for months.
implementation_guidance:
Define the triggers that force an out-of-cycle risk review: onboarding a subprocessor that touches customer data, a major architecture or hosting change, a new data type or jurisdiction, the start of any project that changes systems, data, sites or suppliers, or significant organizational change.
Hold a project's review at its planning stage, and in every case complete the triggered review before the change goes live, not after.
Document each review, its conclusion and any new risks added to the register.
Review the trigger list annually so it keeps pace with the business.
name: Change-triggered risk review

evidence.name: Procedure listing what triggers a risk review
evidence.what: Procedure for risk reviews after a change
evidence.where: A section of the risk method, kept in the Documents module.
evidence.shows: Triggers such as a new product, vendor, country, major incident or acquisition, and who runs the review.

evidence.name: Risk reviews done after significant changes
evidence.what: Risk reviews done after significant changes
evidence.where: Risks module entries updated after each trigger, with the change noted.
evidence.shows: Date, the change that triggered the review, risks added or rescored, and who took part.
evidence.if_none: A dated note from the risk owner that no trigger event happened in [period].

description: Controls exist to mitigate identified risks. Without an explicit mapping it cannot be shown that every material risk is addressed, nor can it be known which risks a failing control leaves exposed.
implementation_guidance:
Maintain a mapping from each risk in the register to the controls that mitigate it.
Flag any risk with no mitigating control, and any control that maps to no risk.
Require a documented acceptance decision, signed by the risk owner, for risks deliberately left unmitigated.
Revisit the mapping whenever a control is disabled or a new risk is added.
name: Risk-to-control mapping

evidence.name: Risks linked to the controls that mitigate them
evidence.what: Risks linked to their controls
evidence.where: Risks module, where each risk lists the controls that reduce it.
evidence.shows: Every treated risk with at least one linked control, and the status of each linked control.

description: Application controls rest on general technology controls. Where access, change management or operations are weak on any system in the footprint, every control depending on that system inherits the weakness.
implementation_guidance:
Inventory the full technology footprint, including systems introduced through acquisition or adopted informally.
Confirm each system is covered by access control, change management and operations controls.
Document any system deliberately out of scope, with the rationale and any compensating controls.
Reconcile the inventory against billing and identity-provider records to find systems nobody registered.
name: IT general controls coverage

evidence.name: Inventory of in scope systems and the general controls over each
evidence.what: In scope system list with the controls over each
evidence.where: A sheet or Assets module export of production systems, each mapped to its access, change and operations controls.
evidence.shows: Each in scope system, its owner, and the access, change, backup and monitoring controls that cover it.

evidence.name: Review that every system is covered by access, change and operations controls
evidence.what: Annual coverage review of in scope systems
evidence.where: A dated review sheet completed by the security lead against the system list.
evidence.shows: Date, reviewer, each system checked, any gap found, and the task raised to close it.

description: Policies are how control expectations are deployed consistently across the organization. A gap in the policy set marks an area where practice is undefined and therefore cannot be shown to operate consistently.
implementation_guidance:
Maintain the core policy set: information security, access control, change management, incident response, business continuity and disaster recovery, vendor management, cloud service use, data handling, acceptable use with clear desk and clear screen rules, remote working including the care of equipment and media taken off site, and secure development.
Ensure each policy is formally approved, versioned and dated, with the top level information security policy approved by top management, or by the board where a regulator requires it, and each topic policy by its accountable manager. The top level policy states the security objectives or how they are set, and commits to meeting applicable legal, regulatory and contractual requirements and to improving the program.
Map each policy to the framework requirements it supports so coverage gaps are visible.
Make the current set available to all staff at a known location, and share the top level policy with customers, regulators or other parties where they need it.
name: Security policy suite

evidence.name: Published security policies covering each required topic
evidence.what: Set of published security policies
evidence.where: Documents module, written from the policy templates and published to staff.
evidence.shows: A policy for each required topic, each with owner, version, approval date and next review date.

evidence.name: Approval record for each policy
evidence.what: Approval record for each policy
evidence.where: The approval step in the Documents module.
evidence.shows: Policy, version, approver and approval date.

description: Policies that no longer describe how the organization actually operates are among the most common audit exceptions. An annual review forces each policy to be read against current practice, re-approved by an accountable owner, and corrected where the two have drifted apart.
implementation_guidance:
Review every policy at least annually, and sooner after a material change to the business or environment.
Record the reviewer, the review date and the outcome, even where the outcome is no change.
Re-approve through the documented approval path rather than editing in place.
Retain superseded versions so the version history can be traced at audit.
name: Annual policy review

evidence.name: Review and re approval record for each policy
evidence.what: Annual review and re approval of each policy
evidence.where: The review step in the Documents module, done once a year for each policy.
evidence.shows: Policy, reviewer, review date, changes made or "no change", and the re approval date.

description: Controls are relied on for a period, not a date. They must therefore be shown to operate throughout that period, which point-in-time checks cannot demonstrate. Ongoing evaluation is what moves a control from designed to operating effectively.
implementation_guidance:
Run automated checks continuously against connected systems, and on a set schedule with the organization's own tools for systems that cannot be connected, and retain each result with its timestamp, so the operating history is preserved.
Route failures to the named control owner with a remediation SLA.
Review recurring failures for design weakness instead of closing each occurrence individually.
Record periods where monitoring itself was unavailable, as that is a gap in the operating evidence.
name: Continuous control monitoring

evidence.name: Control test results across the period under review
evidence.what: Control check results for the period
evidence.where: The Controls module check history, kept across the whole audit period.
evidence.shows: Each control check with the dates it ran, the result, and how long any failure lasted.

evidence.name: Exceptions found by monitoring and how they were resolved
evidence.what: Failed checks and how they were fixed
evidence.where: Tasks module, one task per failed check, raised from the control page.
evidence.shows: Failed check, date found, owner, fix and date closed.
evidence.if_none: The check history showing no failures in [period].

description: A penetration test is an adversarial evaluation of controls as they actually run rather than as they are documented. It surfaces exploitable weaknesses that scanning and self-assessment consistently miss.
implementation_guidance:
Commission an independent penetration test at least annually and after major architectural change, and before it starts agree the scope, timing, test accounts and any tests that could disrupt service with the system owner in writing.
Scope it to cover internet-facing applications and infrastructure and, where systems run on premises or handle card data, the internal network and the controls that separate the card data environment, using a tester independent of the team that runs those systems, and state any exclusions in the report.
Track findings to remediation against a severity-based SLA.
Obtain retest confirmation for high and critical findings, and retain the report and attestation letter.
name: Annual penetration test

evidence.name: Penetration test report from an independent tester
evidence.what: Penetration test report
evidence.where: Delivered by the outside testing firm, usually as a PDF.
evidence.shows: Tester name and firm, dates, scope, method, each finding with severity, and a summary.

evidence.name: Remediation of findings, with retest evidence
evidence.what: Pen test findings fixed and retested
evidence.where: Vulnerabilities module, one entry per finding, closed with the tester's retest letter or report.
evidence.shows: Each finding, owner, fix date, retest result, and the approval for any risk accepted instead of fixed.
evidence.if_none: The report showing no findings, or only informational ones.

evidence.name: Rules of engagement agreed in writing before each test
evidence.what: Signed rules of engagement for the pen test
evidence.where: The scope letter or statement of work signed with the testing firm before testing starts.
evidence.shows: Targets, dates, test types allowed, contacts, how to stop the test in an emergency, and signatures from both sides.

description: An internal audit, run on a set program by people who do not audit their own work, tests whether the security program and its controls operate as documented. It finds gaps while there is time to fix them and feeds its findings into corrective action and management review.
implementation_guidance:
Keep an internal audit program that sets how often each part of the security program is audited, based on its importance and the results of earlier audits, the methods used, and who plans, performs and reports each audit, so the whole program, management processes as well as controls, is audited at least once a year and ahead of each external audit, with a targeted review after significant change to the business, systems or program.
For each audit, record the scope, the criteria, such as internal policies, contracts and the standards the organization works to, the method, the evidence examined and the findings, not just a conclusion.
Choose auditors who do not audit their own work, and use another team or an outside reviewer where the security team is too small to keep that separation, rather than having owners assess their own controls.
Report results to the managers responsible, to management review and, where one exists, to the audit committee, and route findings into deficiency tracking so remediation is managed like any other finding.
name: Internal audit

evidence.name: Internal audit program setting frequency, methods, responsibilities and criteria
evidence.what: Internal audit program
evidence.where: Documents module, written by the security lead or an outside reviewer.
evidence.shows: What is audited, how often, methods, who audits and how they stay independent, and how findings are reported.

evidence.name: Internal audit report with scope, criteria, evidence examined and findings
evidence.what: Internal audit report
evidence.where: Written by an outside reviewer, or by a staff member who does not own the controls audited.
evidence.shows: Scope, criteria, dates, auditor, evidence examined, findings, and who received the report.

evidence.name: Remediation plan for the gaps found
evidence.what: Remediation plan for internal audit findings
evidence.where: Tasks module, one task per finding.
evidence.shows: Each finding with the action, owner, due date and status.
evidence.if_none: The audit report stating that no findings were raised.

description: Identifying a deficiency is only half the control; the other half is communicating it to those responsible and getting it corrected. Untracked findings recur, and a pattern of repeat findings is itself an audit exception.
implementation_guidance:
Record every finding from audits, tests, monitoring, incidents and complaints in one tracker with an owner, severity, the immediate fix or containment and how its consequences were handled, root cause and due date.
Drive due dates from a severity-based SLA rather than negotiating each one, and check whether the same cause could exist in other systems, teams or controls.
Require closure evidence rather than self-attestation before a finding is closed, and confirm the action worked, for significant findings by checking after a set period that the problem has not returned.
Escalate items that age past their SLA to management review, and update policies, procedures or controls when the cause shows the program itself needs to change.
name: Deficiency remediation tracking

evidence.name: Log of control deficiencies with owner, due date and closure
evidence.what: Control deficiency log
evidence.where: Tasks module, with each deficiency raised as a task, or the ticket tracker such as Jira or Linear.
evidence.shows: Each deficiency with its source, date found, owner, due date, status and date closed.
evidence.if_none: A dated note from the security lead that no deficiencies were found in [period].

evidence.name: Communication of deficiencies to the people responsible
evidence.what: Notice of each deficiency to the people responsible
evidence.where: The email, Slack message or meeting note that told the owner and leadership.
evidence.shows: Deficiency, who was told, date, and the due date given.
evidence.if_none: A dated note from the security lead that no deficiencies were found in [period].

description: Obligations arrive from contracts, regulation and certification commitments, and each changes independently of the others. A single register turns a scattered set of promises into a managed list, so an obligation is not discovered only when it has been breached.
implementation_guidance:
Maintain a register of every applicable legal, regulatory and contractual obligation with its source, owner and review date.
Map each obligation to the controls that satisfy it, so coverage gaps are visible.
Review the register at least annually and whenever entering a new market or signing commitments with new requirements.
Assign a named owner to each obligation rather than to the register as a whole.
name: Compliance obligations register

evidence.name: Register of contractual, regulatory and certification obligations
evidence.what: Compliance obligations register
evidence.where: A sheet kept by the security lead or a founder, built from contracts, laws and certifications.
evidence.shows: Each obligation with its source, owner, what it requires, and the control that meets it.

evidence.name: Review of the register for new obligations
evidence.what: Annual review of the obligations register
evidence.where: A dated review note, or the change history of the register sheet.
evidence.shows: Date, reviewer, new contracts, laws and certifications checked, and the changes made.

description: Policies only influence behavior if staff can find them and know they apply. Acknowledgement is the evidence that expectations were communicated, and without it a policy breach can be met with the claim that nobody was told.
implementation_guidance:
Publish the current policy set where all staff can access it without needing to ask.
Track acknowledgement at hire and on material change, per person and per policy.
Communicate changes actively rather than relying on staff to notice a new version.
Follow up outstanding acknowledgements, escalating persistent non-completion.
name: Internal policy portal

evidence.name: Policy portal showing current policies available to staff
evidence.what: Screenshot of the staff policy portal
evidence.where: The Documents module staff view, or the shared drive or wiki page where policies are published.
evidence.shows: The current version of each policy, visible to all staff, with dates.

evidence.name: Staff acknowledgement of current policies
evidence.what: Staff acknowledgement of current policies
evidence.where: Documents module acknowledgement campaign, sent at hire and once a year.
evidence.shows: Each person on the staff list, the policies acknowledged, and the date.

description: Staff and customers often notice incidents before monitoring does. A known, low-friction reporting channel is what converts that observation into an alert instead of a private concern.
implementation_guidance:
Operate a dedicated reporting channel, such as a security alias or a monitored chat channel.
Communicate it at onboarding, in training and in the incident-response plan.
Monitor it during defined hours and route reports into the triage process.
Encourage reporting of suspicion rather than certainty, and respond without blame so people keep reporting.
name: Security incident reporting channel

evidence.name: Published reporting channel for staff and customers
evidence.what: Published security reporting channel
evidence.where: The security page on the website, a security.txt file, and the staff handbook or wiki.
evidence.shows: An address or form such as security@, who reads it, the expected response time, for both staff and customers.

evidence.name: List of all security reports received in the period, with date, source, summary, decision and date closed. The auditor chooses the sample from it.
evidence.what: List of security reports received in the period
evidence.where: The shared inbox behind security@, or the tickets created from it.
evidence.shows: Every report with date received, who sent it, summary, triage decision and date closed.
evidence.if_none: A dated note: "no security reports received in [period]", with a screenshot of the empty inbox or ticket filter.

description: A confidential reporting path allows misconduct to be raised where the normal management line is part of the concern. Without it, such concerns go unreported, and the organization's commitment to integrity and accountability cannot be shown to work in practice.
implementation_guidance:
Provide a confidential and, where practical, anonymous reporting mechanism.
Document how reports are received, investigated and escalated, and who is excluded from handling a report about themselves.
Communicate the mechanism to all staff and state the prohibition on retaliation.
Record reports and their handling confidentially, and report volume to the oversight body.
name: Whistleblower / ethics reporting mechanism

evidence.name: Description of the confidential reporting mechanism
evidence.what: Description of the confidential reporting channel
evidence.where: A section of the employee handbook, or the page of an outside hotline service.
evidence.shows: How to report, that reports can be anonymous, who receives them, and protection from retaliation.

evidence.name: Anonymized log of reports received and outcomes
evidence.what: Anonymized log of ethics reports and outcomes
evidence.where: Kept by the person who receives reports, or exported from the hotline service.
evidence.shows: Date, category, investigation steps, outcome and date closed, with no names.
evidence.if_none: A dated note from the person who receives reports: "no reports received in [period]".

description: Customers are entitled to know the security, availability and privacy commitments being made to them. Those published commitments are also obligations the controls must meet and auditors will test against, so they must match reality.
implementation_guidance:
Publish terms of service, service level commitments, a security or trust page and a privacy notice.
Ensure published commitments match what the controls actually deliver, as an overstated commitment creates an exception.
Review published material at least annually and after material change to the service.
Record approval of changes to committed terms.
name: External security commitments

evidence.name: Published security, availability and privacy commitments
evidence.what: Published security, availability and privacy commitments
evidence.where: The security page, terms of service, SLA, privacy policy and standard customer contract.
evidence.shows: Copies or links of each, with dates, showing what is promised on security, uptime and privacy.

evidence.name: Check that the commitments match actual practice
evidence.what: Annual check that public promises match practice
evidence.where: A sheet by the security lead comparing each promise with how the system really works.
evidence.shows: Each promise, the control or setting that meets it, the result, and any page or practice changed.

description: Breach-notification commitments made in customer contracts are binding and time-bound. If those timeframes are not known to the people running an incident, they will be missed.
implementation_guidance:
Document the breach-notification timeframes committed to customers, including any variation by contract.
Make the shortest applicable commitment the operating standard for the incident process.
Build the customer notification decision into the incident-response plan as an explicit step with an owner.
Maintain current notification contacts for each customer and verify them periodically.
name: Customer breach-notification commitment

evidence.name: Customer contract terms on breach notification
evidence.what: Breach notice clause in the customer contract
evidence.where: The standard customer agreement or data processing agreement.
evidence.shows: The clause with the notice timeframe, what customers are told, and who is told.

evidence.what: Incident procedure with customer notice timeframes
evidence.where: The incident response plan in the Documents module.
evidence.shows: Notice timeframes that match the contract, who decides, who sends the notice, and the template used.

description: Background screening is the control that applies before trust is extended. Once someone holds production access, the opportunity to verify suitability has already passed.
implementation_guidance:
Run background checks, where legally permitted, before granting access to production or customer data, and again before someone moves into a more sensitive role.
Define the check scope by role, applying deeper screening to privileged and finance-facing positions, and repeat or refresh checks for those roles at an interval you set from risk and law, recorded in the screening policy.
Apply the same standard to contractors who receive equivalent access, through the contract with their employer where you cannot screen them yourself.
Retain evidence that the check was completed and cleared, without retaining unnecessary personal detail.
name: Pre-hire background checks

evidence.name: Background check policy stating the scope for each role and the recheck interval
evidence.what: Background check policy
evidence.where: Documents module, usually a section of the HR or personnel security policy.
evidence.shows: Which checks apply to which roles, that checks finish before access is given, the recheck interval, and who reviews results.

evidence.shows: Every hire, role change and recheck with name, role, start date, date the check finished and whether it cleared.
evidence.if_none: A dated note from HR that no one was hired, changed role or was due a recheck in [period].

description: Staff are the most frequently targeted attack surface, primarily through phishing and social engineering. Training is the control that turns the workforce from the weakest link into a detection layer.
implementation_guidance:
Deliver security awareness training at onboarding and at least annually thereafter, to employees and to contractors with access to company systems or data.
Cover phishing, social engineering, credential handling, data classification and incident reporting, and add role-based modules where a role needs more, such as secure coding for engineers and privileged access handling for administrators.
Track completion to 100 percent and escalate non-completion rather than letting it lapse.
Supplement with periodic phishing simulation, using results to target training rather than to penalize.
name: Security awareness training

evidence.name: Training content and schedule
evidence.what: Security awareness training content and schedule
evidence.where: The course list in the training platform, or the slide deck used, with the yearly plan.
evidence.shows: Topics such as phishing, passwords, data handling and incident reporting, who must take it, and when.

evidence.name: Completion records for all staff
evidence.what: Training completion report for all staff
evidence.where: Exported from the training platform, or a sign off sheet for a session run in house.
evidence.shows: Each person on the staff list, the course, completion date, and follow up for anyone overdue.

description: Competence can only be judged against what a role requires, so that has to be defined first. Where security duties are not written into the role, they are nobody's job in particular.
implementation_guidance:
Maintain role descriptions stating required qualifications, experience and responsibilities.
State the security responsibilities attached to each role explicitly.
Use the description as the basis for the access the role receives.
Review descriptions when roles change materially, and align them with the control ownership map.
name: Job descriptions with security responsibilities

evidence.name: Job descriptions that state security responsibilities
evidence.what: Job descriptions with security duties
evidence.where: The HR tool or shared drive, often the same text used in job posts.
evidence.shows: A security duties section in each role, such as following policies and reporting incidents, plus extra duties for technical roles.

description: Onboarding is the one moment when a new joiner will reliably complete required steps. Agreements, policy acknowledgement, training and correctly scoped access are far harder to collect afterwards.
implementation_guidance:
Use a per-hire checklist covering signed agreements, policy acknowledgement, security training assignment and access request and approval.
Provision access from the role definition rather than by copying another user.
Complete security training within a defined period from the start date.
Record completion per item so onboarding can be evidenced for any individual.
name: Onboarding checklist

evidence.name: Onboarding checklist
evidence.what: Onboarding checklist template
evidence.where: A checklist in the HR tool, a ticket template or a shared doc.
evidence.shows: Steps such as contract signed, background check, policy acknowledgement, training, device setup and approved access.

evidence.name: List of all new joiners in the period, with name, role, start date and checklist completion date. The auditor chooses the sample from it.
evidence.what: List of new joiners with checklist completion dates
evidence.where: HR tool export of joiners, with the completed checklist or ticket for each.
evidence.shows: Every joiner in the period with start date and the date each checklist step was done.
evidence.if_none: A dated note from HR that no one joined in [period], with the HR tool export.

description: Departures are the highest-risk transition in the access lifecycle. Retained access after departure is both a common audit exception and a common breach vector, and ownership of documents and accounts is easily lost with the person.
implementation_guidance:
Use a documented offboarding checklist covering access revocation, return of devices, badges, physical keys and hardware tokens, credential rotation, transfer of document and account ownership, reassignment of any custodian duty such as key components or safe combinations with any combination the person knew changed, and a written reminder of the duties that continue after exit, such as confidentiality, acknowledged by the leaver.
Trigger it from the HR system on termination, and run the relevant access, asset and duty items when someone changes role, so rights, assets and duties from the old role do not carry over.
Revoke access within a defined SLA, measured in hours for involuntary departures.
Verify and record completion per item rather than marking the checklist done as a whole.
name: Offboarding and deprovisioning

evidence.name: Offboarding checklist
evidence.what: Offboarding checklist template
evidence.where: A checklist in the HR tool, a ticket template or a shared doc.
evidence.shows: Steps such as disable sign in, remove app access, return or wipe the device, rotate shared secrets, and the timeframe for each.

evidence.name: Completed offboarding records for leavers in the period
evidence.what: Completed offboarding record for each leaver
evidence.where: The checklist or ticket closed for each leaver.
evidence.shows: Leaver, last day, each step done with its date, and who did it.
evidence.if_none: A dated note from HR that no one left in [period], with the HR tool export.

evidence.name: Roster of joiners and leavers with dates
evidence.what: Joiner and leaver list with dates
evidence.where: Exported from the HR tool or payroll.
evidence.shows: Every joiner and leaver in the period with name, role, start date and end date.

description: Confidentiality agreements make the obligation to protect customer and company information legally binding and enforceable, rather than a matter of expectation.
implementation_guidance:
Require a signed confidentiality and intellectual property agreement from every employee and contractor, and a non-disclosure agreement from any other outside party, such as a partner or prospective supplier, before they receive confidential information or access.
Include a security clause in each employment contract and contractor agreement that states the person's security duties and the organization's duties to them, refers to the policies they must follow and states the consequence of a breach.
Ensure obligations survive termination of the engagement, and track signature status centrally so completeness can be evidenced per person and per party.
Review the templates at least annually against what needs protecting, and refresh agreements when scope of access or applicable law changes materially.
name: Confidentiality / IP agreements

evidence.name: Confidentiality and IP agreement, non-disclosure agreement and contract security clause templates, with the record of their annual review
evidence.what: Confidentiality, IP and NDA templates with their annual review
evidence.where: Documents module, holding the templates kept by a founder or the company lawyer.
evidence.shows: The employee and contractor agreement, the NDA and the contract security clause, each with its review date.

evidence.name: List of all staff, contractors and outside parties who started in the period, with name, agreement type and date signed. The auditor chooses the sample from it.
evidence.what: List of people and outside parties with signed agreements
evidence.where: HR tool export of people, with signed agreements from the signing tool such as DocuSign.
evidence.shows: Every person and outside party who started in the period, agreement type, and date signed.
evidence.if_none: A dated note that no staff, contractors or outside parties started in [period].

description: Performance management is how competence is maintained rather than assumed. It is where skills gaps, including security-relevant ones, are identified and where accountability for control responsibilities is reinforced.
implementation_guidance:
Run a documented performance evaluation for every employee at least annually.
Assess against clear expectations for the role, including its security responsibilities.
Identify skills gaps and record the resulting training or development actions.
Retain the record of the review, handled confidentially through HR.
name: Performance management

evidence.name: Performance review process
evidence.what: Performance review process
evidence.where: Guidance for managers in the HR tool or shared drive.
evidence.shows: How often reviews happen, who reviews, and that security duties are part of the review.

evidence.name: Completed reviews showing control responsibilities were assessed
evidence.what: Completed performance reviews that cover security duties
evidence.where: Exported from the HR tool, or the review form for each person.
evidence.shows: Person, reviewer, date, and comments on security or control duties.

description: Contractors carry the same access risk as employees but sit outside the HR lifecycle that normally triggers onboarding and offboarding. That gap is where forgotten access accumulates.
implementation_guidance:
Track every contractor in a register with sponsor, scope of access and a mandatory end date.
Apply the same onboarding requirements: agreements, policy acknowledgement, training and approved access.
Trigger deprovisioning and the return of company devices, badges and data automatically from the end date, record each item returned, and require positive action to extend.
Include contractors in access reviews rather than reviewing employees alone.
name: Contractor lifecycle management

evidence.name: Contractor onboarding and offboarding procedure
evidence.what: Contractor onboarding and offboarding procedure
evidence.where: Shared drive, often part of the onboarding and offboarding checklists.
evidence.shows: Agreement signed before access, who sponsors the contractor, access given, end date, and removal on exit.

evidence.name: Contractor register with start and end dates and access
evidence.what: Contractor register
evidence.where: A sheet or HR tool list kept by operations.
evidence.shows: Each contractor with company, sponsor, start date, end date, and the systems they can reach.
evidence.if_none: A dated note that no contractors were engaged in [period].

description: Centralizing authentication through one identity provider makes access consistently governed: policy is enforced in one place, and revocation on departure actually reaches every application rather than the ones somebody remembered.
implementation_guidance:
Route access to every system that supports SAML or OIDC through the identity provider.
Enforce MFA, session and password policy centrally at the provider so applications inherit them.
Maintain a documented list of systems that cannot support SSO, with compensating controls for each.
Verify that deprovisioning at the provider removes application access, and check the exceptions explicitly.
name: Enforce single sign-on

evidence.name: Approved exceptions for applications outside single sign on
evidence.what: Approved list of applications outside single sign on
evidence.where: A sheet kept by the IT lead, with an approval for each app that cannot use single sign on.
evidence.shows: Each app, the reason, the safeguard used instead such as password manager and second factor, approver and date.
evidence.if_none: A dated note from the IT lead: "every in scope application used single sign on in [period]".

description: Passwords alone fail against phishing, reuse and credential-stuffing, and stolen credentials remain the most common initial access vector. Multi-factor authentication is the single highest-value access control available.
implementation_guidance:
Require MFA for all users on all systems that support it, with no standing exclusions.
Require phishing-resistant factors such as WebAuthn or hardware keys for administrators and for access to production.
Prioritize systems holding sensitive data and systems controlling network, infrastructure or production if a phased rollout is unavoidable.
Monitor for accounts that bypass or disable MFA, and treat enrolment gaps as findings.
name: Enforce multi-factor authentication

evidence.name: Access policy requiring multi factor authentication
evidence.what: Access policy requiring a second factor
evidence.where: Documents module, in the access control policy.
evidence.shows: Which systems require a second factor, the methods allowed, and how exceptions are approved.

evidence.name: Approved exceptions to multi factor authentication
evidence.what: Approved exceptions to multi factor authentication
evidence.where: A sheet kept by the IT lead, with an approval for each account.
evidence.shows: Each account or app, the reason, the safeguard used instead, approver, date and expiry.
evidence.if_none: A dated note from the IT lead: "no exceptions to multi factor authentication in [period]".

evidence.where: Exported from the identity provider such as Google Workspace, Microsoft Entra or Okta. Upload it until a connector collects it.

description: Password policy is the baseline that protects accounts where stronger factors are unavailable. Modern guidance favours length and breach-checking over forced rotation and complexity rules, which drive predictable, weaker passwords.
implementation_guidance:
Enforce the policy centrally at the identity provider rather than per application.
Set a minimum length of at least 12 characters, screen new passwords against known breach corpora, and make initial and reset passwords unique, single use and changed at first login.
Avoid mandatory periodic rotation unless a credential is known or suspected to be compromised, or a regulation or contract you are bound by requires it, for example a change at least every 90 days where a password is the only factor protecting card data and account risk is not analyzed continuously.
Lock accounts after no more than ten failed attempts, for at least 30 minutes or until the user's identity is confirmed, or apply equivalent rate limiting where lockout is not available, and verify the person's identity through a separate channel before resetting a password or second factor.
name: Password policy

evidence.name: Password policy
evidence.what: Password policy
evidence.where: Documents module, often part of the access control policy.
evidence.shows: Minimum length, reuse rules, lockout, when passwords must change, and a ban on sharing.

description: Some credentials cannot be replaced by single sign-on, and those are exactly the ones that end up in spreadsheets, chat messages and browser profiles. A managed password manager gives them a controlled home with auditable sharing.
implementation_guidance:
Provide a company password manager and require its use for all shared and non-SSO credentials.
Organize secrets into vaults scoped by team and role rather than one shared vault.
Prohibit credential sharing over chat or email in the acceptable use policy.
Revoke vault access at offboarding, and rotate any shared credential the departing person could read.
name: Company password manager

evidence.what: Policy requiring the company password manager

description: Granting access per person produces entitlements nobody can reason about. Defining access by role makes least privilege reviewable, repeatable, and correct by default when someone joins or changes job.
implementation_guidance:
Define roles or groups that map to job functions, and grant access to roles rather than to individuals.
Base each role on the minimum access the function requires, and document what that is.
Provision new joiners from the role definition instead of copying an existing user's access.
Review role definitions periodically, as roles accumulate permissions the same way individuals do.
name: Role-based access and least privilege

evidence.what: Role and access matrix

evidence.name: Role definitions approved by their owners

evidence.where: An email, ticket or signed sheet from each system owner.
evidence.shows: Each role or group, the owner who approved it, and the date.

evidence.name: Export of groups or roles and their members for each in scope system
evidence.what: Group and role membership export for each in scope system
evidence.where: Exported from the identity provider, the cloud console, source control and the product admin panel.
evidence.shows: Date, each system, each group or role and its members, matching the role and access matrix.

description: Access granted without a recorded authorization cannot be shown to be appropriate, and it is the point at which least privilege is either enforced or quietly abandoned. The approval record is what an auditor samples to test the control.
implementation_guidance:
Require a documented request and approval before any account or entitlement is created, give each person an account of their own, and allow shared or generic accounts only by approved exception with a named owner.
Route approval to the system or data owner rather than to the requester's manager alone for privileged access.
Capture the business justification, so the grant can be re-evaluated at the next access review.
Provision only after approval is recorded, and reject retrospective approvals as a matter of process.
name: Access provisioning approval

evidence.name: Access request and approval procedure
evidence.what: Access request and approval procedure
evidence.where: Documents module, in the access control policy.
evidence.shows: How access is requested, who approves for each system, and that approval comes before access is given.

evidence.name: List of all access granted in the period, with requester, approver, date and system. The auditor chooses the sample from it.
evidence.what: List of access granted with requester and approver
evidence.where: The ticket tracker or access request tool, exported for the period.
evidence.shows: Every access grant with system, person, requester, approver, approval date and grant date.

description: The window between someone losing authorization and losing access is a window of unmonitored risk. Departures are also when access is most likely to be used inappropriately.
implementation_guidance:
Trigger deprovisioning automatically from the HR or identity system on termination or role change.
Define an SLA measured in hours for revoking access on involuntary termination.
Cover systems outside SSO, shared credentials, VPN, code repositories and physical access.
Reconcile active accounts against active staff periodically, and investigate every account without a current owner.
name: Timely access removal

evidence.name: Access removal procedure with the timeframe
evidence.what: Access removal procedure with timeframe

evidence.shows: Every leaver with last day, the date each account was disabled, and who did it.

description: Access accumulates. People change roles, projects end and temporary grants become permanent, so entitlements that were appropriate when issued drift out of alignment with duties. Periodic recertification is what corrects that drift.
implementation_guidance:
Run access reviews at least annually, and quarterly for production, financial and administrative systems.
Have the system or data owner certify each user individually rather than approving a list in bulk.
Revoke access that is not affirmatively certified, and verify the revocation actually executed.
Retain the review record, the decisions and the evidence of resulting changes.

description: Administrative and root access can disable controls, read all data and erase its own traces. It therefore warrants tighter provisioning, shorter tenure and closer review than standard access.
implementation_guidance:
Maintain an inventory of privileged accounts across every system, including cloud root, break-glass, database, network device and built-in administrator accounts, with a named owner for each, and of the tools that can bypass system or application controls, such as cloud and database admin consoles, container exec access, hypervisor tools and debuggers on production hosts.
Require explicit, separately recorded approval for privileged grants.
Prefer just-in-time elevation over standing administrative rights, do privileged work from a separate account or elevated role rather than the one used for email and browsing, and log every elevation and every use of the listed tools.
Review privileged access quarterly, keep break-glass and shared administrator credentials in a vault with monitored, alerting check-out, and record privileged sessions on the most sensitive systems, such as payment or core banking systems, where the tooling allows.

evidence.where: Exported from the identity provider and the cloud console admin roles.

description: Where one person can initiate, approve and execute the same sensitive action, both fraud and simple error go undetected. Separating those duties introduces a second pair of eyes at the point where it matters.
implementation_guidance:
Identify conflicting duty pairs, such as deploying to production and approving that deployment, creating a vendor and approving its payment, or entering and authorizing a financial transaction.
Separate them in system permissions rather than by convention, and where a system supports it enforce maker checker approval so the person who enters a sensitive action cannot also approve it.
Where team size makes separation impractical, document a compensating control such as independent after-the-fact review of a logged action.
Re-examine separation whenever the team grows or restructures, and check user entitlements against the conflict matrix at least annually, or quarterly for payment and other high-risk financial systems.

description: Service accounts, API keys and tokens authenticate without a human present. They are rarely reviewed, frequently over-permissioned, and often outlive the integration that created them.
implementation_guidance:
Inventory every service account, API key and integration token with its owner, purpose and permissions.
Scope each to least privilege, and never use a provider's default or highly privileged service account.
Rotate credentials on a defined schedule and immediately on suspected exposure.
Review the inventory at least annually and disable accounts with no recent authentication activity.

description: Sessions that never expire turn a single stolen laptop or hijacked token into indefinite access. Session limits bound how long a compromised session remains useful.
implementation_guidance:
Configure idle and absolute session timeouts centrally at the identity provider.
Set shorter timeouts for administrative interfaces and systems holding sensitive data.
Require re-authentication for high-risk actions such as changing MFA settings or granting access.
Ensure logout and deprovisioning invalidate active sessions and refresh tokens, not only future logins.

evidence.where: Session settings in the identity provider and cloud console, and the session setting in the product's configuration.

description: Encryption at rest protects data when the storage layer is exposed through a lost device, a misconfigured snapshot, a decommissioned disk or direct access to the underlying store. It is a baseline expectation for confidential and personal data.
implementation_guidance:
Enable encryption at rest on every data store, including databases, object storage, snapshots, backups and disks.
Use platform-managed keys as the minimum, and customer-managed keys where required by commitment or regulation.
Verify encryption is actually enabled rather than assumed, and monitor for unencrypted resources being created.
Ensure new resources inherit encryption by default through policy or infrastructure as code.
name: Encryption at rest

evidence.name: Encryption standard stating what is encrypted and how
evidence.what: Encryption at rest standard
evidence.where: Documents module, in the cryptography or encryption policy.
evidence.shows: Which data stores are encrypted, the method such as AES 256 through the cloud provider, and who manages the keys.

evidence.name: Encryption setting for every data store, exported from the cloud console
evidence.what: Encryption setting for every data store
evidence.where: Cloud console or CLI export for databases, storage buckets, disks and backups, such as AWS RDS, S3 and EBS.
evidence.shows: Date, every data store in the asset list, encryption turned on, and the key used.

description: Data crossing a network can be intercepted or modified in transit. Transport encryption makes intercepted traffic unusable and authenticates the endpoint being connected to.
implementation_guidance:
Enforce TLS 1.2 or higher on all external endpoints, and disable legacy protocols and weak cipher suites.
Redirect HTTP to HTTPS and enable HSTS so downgrade is not possible.
Require TLS for internal service-to-service traffic and for database connections, not only at the edge.
Monitor certificate expiry and automate renewal so an outage does not create pressure to disable TLS.
name: Encryption in transit (TLS)

evidence.name: Encryption in transit standard
evidence.what: Encryption in transit standard
evidence.where: Documents module, in the cryptography or encryption policy.
evidence.shows: Minimum TLS version, where it applies, how certificates are managed, and what happens to old clients.

evidence.name: Scan result for each public endpoint showing protocol version, and the load balancer settings
evidence.what: TLS scan of each public endpoint with load balancer settings
evidence.where: A free TLS scanner such as SSL Labs or testssl.sh, plus the TLS policy on the load balancer from the cloud console.
evidence.shows: Date, each public domain, the TLS versions accepted, certificate expiry, and the policy set on the load balancer.

description: Encryption reduces to key management. If keys are unprotected, over-shared or never rotated, the encryption they support provides far less assurance than it appears to.
implementation_guidance:
Manage keys in a dedicated KMS or HSM, held separately from the data they protect, and for keys that protect card data, payment messages or interbank links, generate and load them inside an HSM under dual control and split knowledge, record each key ceremony with the named custodians, and have each custodian sign an acknowledgment of their duties.
Restrict key use and administration through policy, and separate those two permissions.
Enable rotation on a defined schedule, define a rotation procedure for compromise, and disable then destroy retired keys only once no data or backup still depends on them, recording each step.
Log and monitor key use, particularly decrypt operations at unusual volume.
name: Encryption key management

evidence.name: Key management policy
evidence.what: Key management policy
evidence.where: Documents module, in the cryptography policy.
evidence.shows: Key types, where keys live such as a cloud KMS, who can use them, rotation intervals, and what to do if a key leaks.

evidence.name: Review of who can use and manage keys
evidence.what: Review of who can use and manage keys
evidence.where: Export of KMS key policies or roles from the cloud console, reviewed and signed.

evidence.name: Key rotation records
evidence.what: Key rotation records
evidence.where: Cloud KMS key settings or rotation history export.
evidence.shows: Each key, its rotation setting, last rotation date, and any manual rotations.

description: Credentials committed to source code, images or configuration are harvested at scale, and they remain valid long after the commit is reverted. Secrets need a managed store with access control and an audit trail.
implementation_guidance:
Store secrets in a dedicated secrets manager or vault, and never in source control, images or environment files in a repository.
Inject secrets at runtime rather than baking them into build artifacts.
Restrict and log access to each secret, and scope access per service.
Rotate any secret on exposure and on a defined schedule, and treat exposure as an incident.
name: Secrets management

evidence.name: Secrets management standard
evidence.what: Secrets management standard
evidence.where: Documents module, in the cryptography or secure development policy.
evidence.shows: Where secrets live such as a secret store, a ban on secrets in code, who can read them, and rotation rules.
