evidence.where: Exported from the secret store, such as AWS Secrets Manager, Vault or Doppler. Never include secret values.
evidence.shows: Date, each secret name, owner, created date, last rotation date, and any past the rotation rule.

description: Flat networks let one compromised host reach everything. Segmentation limits blast radius and keeps data stores off paths that never needed to reach them.
implementation_guidance:
Place databases and internal services in private subnets with no route from the internet.
Define trust zones and control traffic between them with default-deny rules.
Separate production from development and corporate networks, and keep guest and wireless networks apart from internal ones.
Verify segmentation by testing reachability rather than by reading the intended design, at least yearly and after any change to the rules between zones, and every six months where segmentation reduces the scope of card data you handle on behalf of customers.
name: Network segmentation

evidence.name: Network diagram showing segments and allowed paths
evidence.what: Network diagram with segments and allowed paths
evidence.where: Drawn by engineering from the cloud network setup, kept in the wiki or shared drive.
evidence.shows: Networks and subnets, what talks to what, internet entry points, and the date drawn.

evidence.name: Review of the rules between segments
evidence.what: Quarterly review of rules between segments
evidence.where: Export of security groups or network rules, reviewed and signed.
evidence.shows: Date, reviewer, each rule between segments, a keep or remove decision, and the changes made.

evidence.name: Segmentation test results
evidence.what: Segmentation test results
evidence.where: A section of the pen test report, or a scan run from one segment toward another.
evidence.shows: Date, who tested, the paths tried, the expected and actual result, and fixes.

description: A default-allow network is an inventory problem disguised as a security problem: nobody can enumerate what is reachable. Default-deny inverts that, so exposure is deliberate and documented.
implementation_guidance:
Configure firewalls and security groups to deny inbound traffic by default and allow only what is explicitly required.
Review rules for 0.0.0.0/0 on sensitive ports, and justify or remove each occurrence.
Attach an owner and a purpose to every allow rule so stale rules can be identified.
Review rule sets periodically and remove rules for decommissioned services.
name: Default-deny firewall rules

evidence.name: Firewall rule register with owner and purpose for each rule
evidence.what: Firewall rule register
evidence.where: Export of security groups or firewall rules, with an owner and purpose added for each.
evidence.shows: Each rule with source, destination, port, owner and purpose.

evidence.name: Periodic review of firewall rules
evidence.what: Quarterly firewall rule review
evidence.where: The rule register, marked up and signed by the reviewer.
evidence.shows: Date, reviewer, each rule kept or removed, and the changes made.

description: Internet-exposed SSH and RDP are scanned continuously and are a recurring high-severity finding. Management interfaces should never be directly reachable from the public internet.
implementation_guidance:
Block SSH, RDP and database ports from the internet at the security group and firewall level.
Provide access through a VPN, zero-trust proxy, bastion host or a session manager service instead.
Scan the external surface regularly to detect newly exposed management ports.
Alert on any change that opens a management port to a public range.
name: No management ports exposed to the internet

evidence.name: Approved exceptions for exposed management access
evidence.what: Approved exceptions for admin ports open to the internet
evidence.where: A sheet kept by engineering and approved by the security lead.
evidence.shows: Each exposed port, the reason, the safeguard used instead, approver, date and expiry.
evidence.if_none: A dated note from the engineering lead: "no admin ports open to the internet in [period]".

evidence.name: Export of inbound rules showing no admin port open to the internet
evidence.what: Inbound rule export showing admin ports closed to the internet
evidence.where: Security group or firewall export from the cloud console, or a report from a cloud security tool.
evidence.shows: Date, every rule open to the internet, and none on admin ports such as SSH 22, RDP 3389 or database ports.

description: Public services face automated attack traffic continuously. A web application firewall filters common injection and scripting attacks, and upstream DDoS protection absorbs volumetric traffic that would otherwise exhaust capacity.
implementation_guidance:
Front public services with a WAF and DDoS protection such as Cloudflare or AWS WAF and Shield.
Start rules in detection mode, tune out false positives, then enforce.
Ensure the origin cannot be reached directly, bypassing the WAF.
Monitor blocked traffic for genuine attack patterns and feed them into detection.
name: WAF and DDoS protection

evidence.name: Review of web application firewall rules and alerts
evidence.what: Quarterly WAF rules and alerts review
evidence.where: The WAF console such as Cloudflare or AWS WAF, with a short review note.
evidence.shows: Date, reviewer, rules active, top alerts or blocks, and the changes made.

description: Trusting a device because it sits on the corporate network fails the moment that network includes home offices, contractors and personal devices. Access decisions should rest on verified identity and device posture, not location.
implementation_guidance:
Require a VPN or zero-trust access solution with MFA for administrative access to infrastructure.
Base access decisions on user identity and device posture rather than source network alone.
Grant access per application rather than issuing broad network access.
Log access sessions and review them alongside privileged access.
name: VPN / zero-trust remote access

evidence.name: Remote access standard
evidence.what: Remote access standard
evidence.where: Documents module, in the access control or network policy.
evidence.shows: How staff reach internal systems, such as VPN or zero trust access, and the sign in and device rules.

evidence.name: Remote access settings and the member list

evidence.where: Admin console of the VPN or zero trust tool, such as Tailscale, Cloudflare Access or the cloud VPN.
evidence.shows: Date, sign in and second factor settings, device rules, and every member compared with the staff list.

description: Cloud workloads are attacked through the control plane as well as the host: credential misuse, cryptomining, anomalous API calls and public exposure. Detection has to cover that plane, not just the operating system.
implementation_guidance:
Enable a managed threat-detection service such as GuardDuty, Defender for Cloud or Security Command Center across all accounts and regions.
Route findings into the on-call and incident process rather than a dashboard nobody watches.
Tune out known-benign findings deliberately, and record the tuning decisions.
Alert on detection being disabled or on an account being created without it.
name: Infrastructure threat detection

evidence.name: Procedure for responding to threat detection alerts

evidence.shows: Which tool raises alerts such as GuardDuty, who triages, the response time, and when to open an incident.

evidence.name: List of all threat detection alerts in the period, with date, severity, investigator, decision and date closed. The auditor chooses the sample from it.
evidence.what: List of threat detection alerts in the period
evidence.where: Exported from the detection tool such as AWS GuardDuty or Google Security Command Center.
evidence.shows: Every alert with date, severity, who looked at it, the decision and date closed.
evidence.if_none: A dated note: "no threat detection alerts in [period]", with the empty export.

description: Default configurations are built for compatibility, not security. A hardening baseline replaces those defaults with a known-good standard and gives drift something measurable to be measured against.
implementation_guidance:
Apply CIS Benchmarks or an equivalent hardening standard to operating systems, containers, databases, cloud services and network devices such as firewalls, routers, switches and wireless controllers, removing or disabling services and tools a system does not need.
Build baselines into images, infrastructure as code and device configuration templates so new systems start hardened, and back up network device configurations whenever they change.
Document and approve any deviation from the baseline, with the reason.
Check for drift at least quarterly, or continuously where tooling allows, remediate regressions, including network device firmware that has fallen out of vendor support, and review the baselines at least annually and when a new benchmark version is released.
name: Hardening baselines (CIS)

evidence.name: Hardening standard such as CIS or equivalent
evidence.what: Hardening standard
evidence.where: Documents module, pointing to the CIS benchmark or the cloud provider's baseline.
evidence.shows: Which baseline applies to servers, containers and cloud accounts, and how it is checked.

evidence.name: Approved exceptions to the standard
evidence.what: Approved exceptions to the hardening standard
evidence.where: A sheet kept by engineering and approved by the security lead.
evidence.shows: Each setting not met, the system, the reason, the safeguard used instead, approver and expiry.
evidence.if_none: A dated note from the engineering lead: "no exceptions to the hardening standard in [period]".

description: Full-disk encryption is what makes a lost or stolen laptop a hardware loss rather than a data breach, and it is what allows devices to be disposed of without forensic erasure.
implementation_guidance:
Enforce full-disk encryption on all endpoints through MDM policy.
Escrow recovery keys centrally so encrypted devices remain recoverable.
Report compliance from MDM and remediate devices found unencrypted.
Verify encryption before issuing a device and again during periodic compliance checks.
name: Endpoint full-disk encryption

evidence.name: Endpoint encryption policy
evidence.what: Endpoint encryption policy
evidence.where: Documents module, in the endpoint or acceptable use policy.
evidence.shows: That laptops must use full disk encryption such as FileVault or BitLocker, and how it is enforced.

evidence.name: Approved exceptions
evidence.what: Approved exceptions to disk encryption
evidence.where: A sheet kept by the IT lead and approved by the security lead.
evidence.shows: Each device, owner, reason, safeguard used instead, approver and expiry.
evidence.if_none: A dated note from the IT lead: "every device was encrypted in [period]", with the device management report.

description: Endpoints are the most common entry point for malware and the device where credentials and data are most exposed. Detection needs to run on the endpoint itself, where the behaviour occurs.
implementation_guidance:
Deploy endpoint detection and response or anti-malware to every managed endpoint and server.
Enable automatic signature and agent updates, and where removable media is allowed, scan it automatically when it is connected.
Monitor agent health and coverage, treat a device without a healthy agent as an exception to be resolved, and for any system judged not to need anti-malware, such as a mainframe or appliance, record the reason and re-check it at least annually.
Route detections into the incident process rather than leaving them in a product console.
name: Endpoint EDR / anti-malware

evidence.name: Endpoint protection standard
evidence.what: Endpoint protection standard
evidence.where: Documents module, in the endpoint policy.
evidence.shows: Which tool protects devices, that it must run on all of them, and who handles alerts.

evidence.shows: Each alert with date, device, severity, who reviewed it, the action and date closed.
evidence.if_none: A dated note: "no endpoint alerts in [period]", with the empty export.

description: Device management is what makes endpoint controls verifiable rather than advisory. It enforces encryption, patching and screen lock consistently, and provides the remote lock and wipe capability that limits the impact of a lost device.
implementation_guidance:
Enrol all company endpoints in MDM before issuing them to staff.
Enforce baseline policy centrally: encryption, screen lock, patch level and permitted software.
Reconcile enrolled devices against the employee roster to find unmanaged devices.
Define how personally owned devices are handled, either enrolled or denied access to company data.
name: Device management (MDM) enrollment

evidence.name: Device management policy
evidence.what: Device management policy
evidence.where: Documents module, in the endpoint policy.
evidence.shows: That company devices must enroll in device management, what is enforced, and how lost devices are handled.

evidence.name: Inventory of company devices
evidence.what: Company device inventory
evidence.where: Assets module, filled from the device management tool such as Jamf, Kandji or Intune.
evidence.shows: Each device with owner, serial number, OS version, enrollment status and last seen date.

description: Most successful attacks exploit vulnerabilities for which a patch already exists. Timely patching is therefore among the highest-value controls, and it is one of the easiest to let slip.
implementation_guidance:
Define patch SLAs by severity for operating systems, browsers and installed software.
Automate deployment through MDM or a patch management tool rather than relying on user action.
Report compliance against the SLA and follow up devices that fall behind.
Handle critical out-of-band patches through the emergency change path.
name: Patch management

evidence.name: Patch management policy with timeframes
evidence.what: Patch management policy
evidence.where: Documents module, in the vulnerability or operations policy.
evidence.shows: Timeframes for applying patches by severity on laptops and servers, and how exceptions are handled.

evidence.name: Patch compliance report
evidence.what: Monthly patch report
evidence.where: Exported from the device management tool and the server patching or scanning tool.
evidence.shows: Each device or server, its OS version, missing patches, and any that are late.

description: A device that leaves the organization with a departing employee, or is lost, still holds company data and cached credentials. Remote wipe is what closes that exposure when the device cannot be recovered.
implementation_guidance:
Maintain remote wipe capability through MDM on all managed devices.
Issue a wipe for lost or stolen devices and for departing employees who do not return hardware.
Confirm the wipe executed rather than assuming the command succeeded, and retain the confirmation.
Cover the case of a device that never reconnects, by rotating credentials it held.
name: Remote wipe on offboarding / loss

evidence.name: Procedure for lost devices and offboarding
evidence.what: Lost device and leaver wipe procedure
evidence.where: Shared drive, or the offboarding checklist.
evidence.shows: How staff report a lost device, who wipes it and how fast, and how devices are wiped when someone leaves.

evidence.name: Wipe confirmations for recovered or lost devices
evidence.what: Device wipe confirmations
evidence.where: Wipe history in the device management tool, or a reset certificate from the recycler.
evidence.shows: Device, owner, reason, wipe date and who did it.
evidence.if_none: A dated note from the IT lead that no device was lost or returned in [period].

description: An unlocked, unattended device grants full access to whoever is nearby, bypassing every authentication control behind it. Automatic locking is what makes physical proximity insufficient.
implementation_guidance:
Enforce automatic screen lock through MDM policy rather than user preference.
Set a short idle timeout, typically no more than 15 minutes, and require authentication to unlock.
Apply the policy to all device types that access company data.
Report compliance and remediate devices that fall out of policy.
name: Screen lock policy

evidence.name: Screen lock standard
evidence.what: Screen lock standard
evidence.where: Documents module, in the endpoint policy.
evidence.shows: Lock after a set idle time such as 5 minutes, a password on wake, and how it is enforced.

evidence.name: Device management report showing the screen lock setting for each device
evidence.what: Screen lock setting report for each device
evidence.where: The compliance or profile report in the device management tool, such as Jamf, Kandji or Intune.
evidence.shows: Date, every company device, the idle lock time applied, and any device out of line with the standard.

description: Confidential data cannot be protected consistently until it has been identified and labelled. Classification is what lets handling rules, access decisions and retention be applied by rule rather than by individual judgement.
implementation_guidance:
Adopt a classification scheme such as public, internal, confidential and restricted, and give each set of data its level based on its confidentiality, integrity and availability needs and on legal, contractual and customer requirements.
Define handling rules per level covering storage, transmission, sharing and disposal, and for removable media holding restricted data, such as card or core banking data, keep a media log, check it against the media held at least annually, and move media off site only by tracked courier with management approval.
Have each data owner classify their data stores and repositories, not only individual documents, and mark information with its level by a defined method for documents, email, files, media and system records, such as a header, a metadata tag or a sensitivity label, stating when marking may be left out.
Train staff on the scheme and on how to mark information, and reference it in the acceptable use policy.
name: Data classification policy

evidence.name: Data classification policy
evidence.what: Data classification policy
evidence.where: Documents module.
evidence.shows: Levels such as public, internal and confidential, how to label data, and the handling rules for each level.

evidence.name: Classification applied to systems and data stores
evidence.what: Classification set on each system and data store
evidence.where: Assets module, with a classification on each asset.
evidence.shows: Each system or data store with its classification and owner.

description: Data protection begins with knowing what data exists and where it lives. An inventory that is incomplete guarantees that some data is protected by nobody, because nobody knows it is there.
implementation_guidance:
Maintain a data map covering databases, object storage, file shares, analytics platforms and vendor systems.
Record for each store the data categories held, classification, owner, location and retention period.
Note the protections applied to each store, such as encryption, access model and backup treatment.
Refresh the map at least annually and when new systems or vendors are introduced.
name: Data inventory and data map

evidence.name: Data inventory and data map
evidence.what: Data inventory and data map
evidence.where: Assets module, or a sheet of data stores with a flow diagram.
evidence.shows: Each data store, the data types in it, owner and location, and where data flows in and out.

evidence.name: Review that the inventory is complete
evidence.what: Annual data inventory completeness review
evidence.where: A dated review note, made by comparing the inventory with the cloud console, app list and vendor list.
evidence.shows: Date, reviewer, sources compared, stores added or removed, and sign off.

description: Data kept beyond its purpose is pure liability: it expands breach impact, deletion obligations and storage cost without serving the business. Retention that is defined but not enforced technically is retention in name only.
implementation_guidance:
Define a retention period for each data type, based on purpose and legal requirement.
Enforce retention technically through lifecycle rules, TTLs or scheduled purge jobs rather than by manual review, and keep records that law or regulation requires to stay unaltered, such as transaction and audit records, on write once or locked storage for the whole period.
Apply retention to backups, archives and analytics copies, not only primary stores.
Document any legal hold that suspends normal retention, and lift it when the hold ends.
name: Data retention schedule

evidence.name: Data retention schedule
evidence.what: Data retention schedule
evidence.where: Documents module.
evidence.shows: Each data type, how long it is kept, why, and how it is deleted.

evidence.name: Deletion records for data past its retention period
evidence.what: Deletion records for data past its retention period
evidence.where: Logs from the scheduled deletion job, or a ticket for each manual deletion.
evidence.shows: Data type, date range deleted, date run, who or what ran it, and record counts.
evidence.if_none: A dated note that no data reached the end of its retention period in [period], with the schedule.

description: Deletion is only meaningful if the data is actually unrecoverable. Data routinely survives in search indexes, caches, analytics warehouses, vendor systems and backups long after it was deleted from the primary store.
implementation_guidance:
Define a disposal procedure covering primary stores, replicas, search indexes, caches, analytics copies and vendor systems, and also laptops, servers, drives, tapes and removable media that are retired, sold, returned from lease or reissued.
Use the data map and the asset inventory as checklists so no store or device is missed.
Age deleted data out of backups within the documented backup retention window, and state that window in the response to the subject.
Wipe or destroy each device and medium by a method that fits the data it held, so neither company data nor licensed software can be recovered, confirm the result before reuse or disposal, and retain a record of what was disposed of, when and by which method, including certificates from any disposal contractor.
name: Secure data disposal

evidence.name: Secure disposal procedure
evidence.what: Secure disposal procedure
evidence.where: Documents module.
evidence.shows: How data and devices are destroyed, the approved methods, who signs off, and how records are kept.

evidence.name: Disposal records or certificates

evidence.if_none: A dated note from the IT lead that nothing was disposed of in [period].

description: Copying production data into development or staging silently extends the confidentiality boundary to environments with weaker access control, less monitoring and broader developer access. It is a frequent and avoidable exception.
implementation_guidance:
Populate lower environments with masked, synthetic or subset data rather than production copies.
Prohibit production data in lower environments in policy, and make the approved seeding path the easy one.
Scan lower environments periodically for data that looks like production personal information.
Where a production restore is genuinely required, require approval, time-box it and record the justification.

evidence.what: Policy against production data in test and dev
evidence.where: Documents module, in the secure development or data policy.
evidence.shows: That real customer data is not copied to test or dev, and the approved way to make test data.

description: The privacy notice is the commitment against which every other privacy control is judged. Where it describes practices that differ from what the systems actually do, the gap is a finding regardless of how strong the controls are.
implementation_guidance:
Publish a privacy notice covering what is collected, why, the legal basis, who it is shared with, how long it is kept and what rights subjects hold.
Write it to match actual data flows, verified against the data map rather than drafted from a template.
Version and date the notice, and retain prior versions.
Notify subjects of material changes through the channel the notice commits to.
name: Privacy notice

evidence.name: Current privacy notice
evidence.what: Current privacy notice
evidence.where: The privacy policy page on the website.
evidence.shows: What data is collected and why, sharing, retention, rights, how to get in touch, and the last updated date.

evidence.name: Notice change history and how data subjects were told
evidence.what: Privacy notice change history and how people were told
evidence.where: Past versions of the page, with the email or banner that announced each change.
evidence.shows: Each version with date, what changed, and how users were told.

description: Where processing relies on consent, that consent must be freely given, recorded, and as easy to withdraw as it was to give. Consent that cannot be evidenced is equivalent to no consent at all.
implementation_guidance:
Capture consent granularly per purpose rather than as a single blanket agreement.
Store a consent record with timestamp, version of the notice shown, and the method of capture.
Obtain explicit consent where sensitive categories of data are involved.
Honour withdrawal promptly and propagate it to downstream systems and processors.
name: Consent and choice management

evidence.name: Consent records showing when, what and which notice version
evidence.what: Consent records
evidence.where: Product database or consent tool such as a cookie banner provider, exported for the period.
evidence.shows: Each consent with person or ID, date, what was agreed, and the notice version shown.

evidence.name: Consent withdrawal process and records
evidence.what: Consent withdrawal steps and log of withdrawals
evidence.where: Product settings or support tickets where users withdrew consent, with the written steps.
evidence.shows: Each withdrawal with date received, date acted on, and what processing stopped.
evidence.if_none: The written withdrawal steps and a dated note that no one withdrew consent in [period].

description: Data that is never collected cannot be breached, misused or subject to a deletion request. Minimization is the cheapest privacy control available and the one most often skipped.
implementation_guidance:
Map each collection point to the stated purpose it serves, and remove fields that serve none.
Challenge new fields at design review rather than after they are in production.
Keep personal information out of logs, error trackers and analytics events.
Review collected fields periodically and retire those no longer used.
name: Data minimization

evidence.name: Review of each collection point against what is needed
evidence.what: Data minimization review of each collection point
evidence.where: A sheet listing every form, API and import that collects personal data, reviewed once a year.
evidence.shows: Each collection point, the fields collected, why each is needed, and fields removed.

description: Personal information collected for one purpose being used for another is one of the most common privacy failures, and it now arises most often when data is repurposed for analytics or model training.
implementation_guidance:
Restrict access to personal information to roles whose purpose requires it.
Require documented approval before any secondary use, and check it against the purposes disclosed in the notice.
State the position on using customer or personal data for AI and model training explicitly, and enforce it technically.
Review actual data flows against stated purposes at least annually.
name: Limit personal-information use to purpose

evidence.name: Register of the purposes personal information is used for
evidence.what: Register of purposes for personal data
evidence.where: A sheet or the data inventory, kept by the privacy owner.
evidence.shows: Each type of personal data, its purpose, the legal basis, and where the privacy notice states it.

evidence.name: Review of new uses against the stated purposes
evidence.what: Review of new uses of personal data
evidence.where: A dated note or ticket for each feature that uses personal data in a new way.
evidence.shows: Date, the new use, the purpose it falls under or the notice update, and who approved it.
evidence.if_none: A dated note that no new use of personal data was added in [period].

description: Data subjects have the right to access their personal information and, in many regimes, an accounting of who it was disclosed to. These requests carry statutory deadlines and are answered from systems that were rarely designed to answer them.
implementation_guidance:
Operate a documented process with a single intake point and a defined SLA aligned to the applicable regime.
Verify the requester's identity proportionately before disclosing anything.
Compile the response across all systems holding the subject's data, using the data map as the checklist.
Log every request, the response given and the date, so timeliness can be evidenced.
name: Data-subject access request process

evidence.name: Access request procedure
evidence.what: Data subject access request procedure

description: Peer review catches defects and security weaknesses before they reach production and spreads knowledge across the team. Enforced through branch protection, it also produces the authorization trail that change management depends on.
implementation_guidance:
Require a pull request with at least one approving review from someone other than the author.
Enforce it through branch protection, and disable direct pushes to protected branches.
Require status checks to pass before merge, and prohibit self-approval.
Record any use of an administrator override and review those occurrences.

Include tests that validate processing accuracy and completeness where the system processes customer data.

description: Testing in production exposes customer data to unreleased code and makes it impossible to distinguish deliberate change from experiment. Separate environments give changes somewhere to be validated before they carry real consequences.
implementation_guidance:
Maintain distinct development, staging and production environments with separate credentials and accounts.
Promote changes through environments in a controlled sequence rather than deploying directly to production.
Restrict production access to those who require it, and protect development and staging with their own access control, patching and monitoring even where access to them is wider.
Keep production data out of lower environments, using masked or synthetic data instead.

description: Unauthorized change is the most common cause of both outages and security regressions. Requiring changes to be authorized, tested and approved before they reach production is the core of change management.
implementation_guidance:

Apply the same requirement to database migrations, configuration and infrastructure changes, and to software installed or updated directly on servers, not only application code; routine low risk changes such as scheduled patching may run under a standard change approved in advance and reviewed yearly.

Define who may authorize an emergency change and under what circumstances.
Require the reason and the actions taken to be recorded at the time, even if briefly.
Require retrospective review and approval within a defined window, normally the next business day.

description: A documented development lifecycle is how security requirements become routine engineering practice rather than individual habit. It also gives new engineers a defined standard to work to, which is what keeps quality stable as a team grows.
implementation_guidance:

Include security requirements such as secure coding standards, static code analysis in the pipeline, dependency management and secrets handling, and train everyone who writes or reviews code in them when they join and at least yearly.
For each new application, major feature or acquired system, record its security requirements, such as authentication, access, data classification, logging, privacy and legal needs, have them approved at design review before building or buying, and check they are met before release.
Define how changes are approved and released and how emergency changes are handled, and have the engineering lead review the policy annually against the tooling actually in use.

description: Cloud configuration changes take effect immediately and can remove a control silently. Detecting drift from the approved baseline is what turns a one-time hardening exercise into a sustained control.
implementation_guidance:
Monitor cloud configuration continuously against a secure baseline.
Alert on high-risk regressions such as public storage exposure, disabled logging or opened management ports.
Define the remediation path for each alert type, and automate reversion where it is safe to do so.
Review recurring drift for a root cause in the provisioning process.
name: Configuration-change detection

evidence.name: Approved configuration baseline
evidence.what: Approved configuration baseline
evidence.where: Infrastructure as code in the repository, or a baseline document approved by the engineering lead.
evidence.shows: The expected settings for servers, cloud accounts and services, with version and approval date.

evidence.name: Alerts on drift that were investigated
evidence.what: Configuration drift alerts and their investigation
evidence.where: Exported from AWS Config, the infrastructure as code drift check or a cloud security tool, with tickets.
evidence.shows: Each drift alert with date, resource, cause, action and date closed.
evidence.if_none: A dated note: "no drift alerts in [period]", with the empty export.

description: Not every alert is an incident, and the decision between the two is itself a control. Recording that evaluation is what shows events were assessed rather than ignored.
implementation_guidance:
Define severity levels and the criteria that place an event in each.
Triage every security event and record the assessment, including events determined to be benign.
Define escalation paths and response expectations per severity.
Review triage decisions periodically for consistency and for events that were misclassified.
name: Security event evaluation

evidence.name: Event triage procedure
evidence.what: Security event triage procedure
evidence.where: Shared drive, or the on call runbook.
evidence.shows: How events are rated, who decides whether an event is an incident, and how fast.

evidence.name: List of all security events evaluated in the period, with date, source, evaluator and the decision taken. The auditor chooses the sample from it.
evidence.what: List of security events evaluated in the period
evidence.where: The alert or ticket queue where events are triaged.
evidence.shows: Every event with date, source, who evaluated it, the decision whether it is an incident, and date.
evidence.if_none: A dated note: "no security events in [period]", with the empty queue.

description: Incidents are handled under time pressure with incomplete information. A plan written in advance is what makes the response consistent rather than dependent on who happens to be available.
implementation_guidance:
Maintain an incident response plan defining roles, severity levels and the phases of detection, containment, eradication, recovery and lessons learned, and share it with everyone who holds a role in it.
Include internal and external communication steps, naming the parties each kind of incident must reach, such as customers, regulators, law enforcement, card brands or the acquirer, with the notification decision as an explicit gate.
State who may collect evidence during an incident, how logs, disk images and files are captured without changing them, and how each item is stored with a record of who handled it and when.
Keep contacts, escalation paths and vendor support routes current, and review the plan annually and after every significant incident.
name: Incident response plan

evidence.what: Incident response plan
evidence.where: Documents module, written from the incident response plan template.
evidence.shows: Severity levels, roles, steps from detection to closure, communication and notice rules, and contacts.

evidence.where: A page in the runbook or wiki, kept current.
evidence.shows: Incident lead and backups, legal, communications and key vendors, with phone and email.

evidence.where: Tasks module, one task per incident, filtered and exported for the quarter.
evidence.shows: Every incident with date found, severity, summary, owner, notice decision and date closed.
evidence.if_none: A dated note signed by the incident lead: "no security incidents in [period]".

description: The value of an incident is the learning, and that is only realized if the analysis is written down and the corrective actions are tracked. Postmortem records are also the audit trail for how an incident was handled.
implementation_guidance:
Run a postmortem for every significant incident, focused on contributing causes rather than individual blame.
Record the timeline, impact, root cause and detection gap.
Raise corrective actions with named owners and due dates, and track them to closure.
Retain the record, and review recurring themes across incidents.
name: Incident postmortems with actions

evidence.name: Postmortem for each significant incident
evidence.what: Postmortem for each significant incident
evidence.where: Written in the wiki or incident tool after each incident.
evidence.shows: Timeline, cause, impact, what went well or badly, and actions with owners.
evidence.if_none: A dated note: "no significant incidents in [period]", matching the incident register.

evidence.name: Corrective actions tracked to closure
evidence.what: Postmortem actions tracked to closure
evidence.where: Tasks module, one task per action from each postmortem.
evidence.shows: Action, incident, owner, due date and date closed.
evidence.if_none: A dated note that no postmortem raised actions in [period].

description: In a period with no incidents, a tabletop exercise is the only operating evidence that the response plan works. It also surfaces the gaps that are otherwise found during a real incident.
implementation_guidance:
Run at least one tabletop exercise annually against a realistic scenario.
Include the people who would actually respond, including engineering, leadership and communications.
Capture what the exercise revealed, particularly gaps in contacts, access and decision authority.
Track resulting actions to closure and retain the record as evidence the plan was exercised.
name: Incident tabletop exercise

evidence.name: Tabletop exercise plan and report
evidence.what: Tabletop exercise plan and report
evidence.where: Written by the security lead after a one or two hour session with the incident team.
evidence.shows: Date, scenario, attendees, decisions made, gaps found and lessons.

evidence.name: Actions from the exercise
evidence.what: Actions from the tabletop exercise
evidence.where: Tasks module, one task per gap found.
evidence.shows: Action, owner, due date and date closed.
evidence.if_none: The exercise report stating that no actions were raised.

description: Recovery is the part of incident response most often left undefined, and it is where improvisation causes the most damage: partial restores, missed credential rotation and reinfection from an unclean backup.
implementation_guidance:
Define recovery procedures covering restoring from backup, rebuilding compromised systems and rotating affected credentials.
Establish criteria for declaring recovery complete and returning to normal operation.
Verify system integrity before restoring service, so a compromise is not reintroduced.
Record the recovery steps performed in each incident record.
name: Incident recovery procedures

evidence.name: Recovery procedures
evidence.what: Incident recovery procedures
evidence.where: Documents module, holding a runbook for restoring each key system.
evidence.shows: Steps to restore service and data, who does them, and how recovery is confirmed.

evidence.name: Recovery records for incidents
evidence.what: Recovery records for incidents
evidence.where: The incident record or ticket, with a timeline of restore steps.
evidence.shows: Incident, systems restored, steps taken, time to recover, and confirmation that it worked.
evidence.if_none: A dated note: "no incidents needed recovery in [period]", matching the incident register.

description: Outages, regional failures and destructive incidents will occur. A plan prepared in advance is what allows recovery within committed timeframes instead of improvising while customers are down.
implementation_guidance:
Maintain a business continuity and disaster recovery plan with defined RTO and RPO per critical service, and record the redundancy each service relies on to meet them, such as multiple availability zones, a secondary site or standby equipment.
Identify critical dependencies, including third parties, and document a workaround for each that keeps the security controls it relies on, such as access control, logging and encryption, in place, or names who may approve a temporary relaxation, what compensates for it and when it must be reversed.
Define activation criteria, roles and communication procedures for customers and staff.
Review and test the plan at least annually, including failover of the redundant components and, where a secondary site or region exists, a switch to it with access control, logging and segmentation confirmed working there, and update it after significant architectural change.
name: Business continuity / disaster recovery plan

evidence.name: Business continuity and disaster recovery plan
evidence.what: Business continuity and disaster recovery plan
evidence.where: Documents module.
evidence.shows: Key services, recovery time and data loss targets, recovery steps, roles, contacts and fallback options.

evidence.what: Continuity or disaster recovery test report

description: Availability commitments are broken by capacity limits reached without warning. Monitoring demand against capacity is what turns a future outage into a planned expansion.
implementation_guidance:
Monitor utilization of compute, storage, network bandwidth, database connections, quotas, rate limits and licenses, and in your own data centers, power, cooling and rack space.
Set alert thresholds below the point of failure, leaving time to act.
Use autoscaling where the workload supports it and test that it engages under load, and for fixed hardware order capacity early enough to cover supplier lead times.
Review capacity trends and provider quotas at least quarterly against forecast growth.
name: Capacity management

evidence.what: Quarterly capacity review record
evidence.where: Monitoring dashboards such as CloudWatch or Datadog, with a short review note.
evidence.shows: Date, reviewer, CPU, memory, storage and quota use against limits, and the growth forecast.

evidence.name: Capacity actions that were taken
evidence.what: Capacity changes made after the review
evidence.where: Tickets or infrastructure changes such as scaling up or raising quotas.
evidence.shows: Change, reason, date and who made it.
evidence.if_none: The review note stating that no capacity changes were needed.

description: Backups are the last defence against ransomware, accidental deletion and regional failure. Automation removes reliance on anyone remembering to run them, and monitoring ensures a silent failure is not discovered during an incident.
implementation_guidance:
Enable automated backups on every production data store, and keep the configuration, infrastructure code and system images needed to rebuild each service, with frequency and retention aligned to the documented RPO.
Encrypt backups at rest and restrict restore permissions to a small, reviewed group.
Alert on backup failure and on jobs that have not completed within the expected window.
Keep at least one copy in a separate region, account or site, protected by immutable storage or held offline, so a single compromise cannot destroy both data and backups.
name: Automated, monitored backups

evidence.name: Backup policy covering scope, frequency and retention
evidence.what: Backup policy
evidence.where: Documents module.
evidence.shows: Which systems and data are backed up, how often, how long copies are kept, where they are stored, and who monitors.

evidence.name: Backup failure alerts and follow up
evidence.what: Backup failure alerts and follow up
evidence.where: Backup tool or cloud backup job history, with a ticket for each failure.
evidence.shows: Each failed job with date, cause, fix, and the date of the next good backup.
evidence.if_none: The backup job history showing every job succeeded in [period].

description: A backup that has never been restored is an assumption, not a control. Restore testing is what converts it into a demonstrated recovery capability and surfaces the gaps before they matter.
implementation_guidance:
Perform a full restore test at least annually and after significant changes to the data platform, and where backups are held on tape or on premises, or a regulator expects it, also restore a sample of systems or files at least quarterly.
Restore into an isolated environment and validate data completeness and integrity, not just job success.
Measure actual restore time against the documented RTO and RPO.
Record the test date, scope, result and any corrective actions.
name: Backup restore testing

evidence.name: Restore test plan and results
evidence.what: Restore test plan and results
evidence.where: Written by engineering after a yearly restore from backup into a test environment.
evidence.shows: Date, what was restored, the steps, who did it, the result and issues found.

evidence.name: Measured recovery time against the target
evidence.what: Measured recovery time compared with the target
evidence.where: Part of the restore test report.
evidence.shows: Target recovery time, actual time, data loss compared with the target, and actions if a target was missed.

description: Third-party risk cannot be managed against an unknown population. The vendor register is the base list that due diligence, agreements and access reviews all work from.
implementation_guidance:
Maintain a vendor register with owner, service provided, criticality, the data each vendor can access and, where a regulator defines it, whether the arrangement is material outsourcing that needs notice to or approval from that regulator.
Reconcile it against accounts payable and identity-provider records to find unregistered vendors.
Record contract dates and renewal points so review happens before commitments auto-renew.
Review the register at least annually and remove vendors no longer in use, confirming their access is revoked.
name: Vendor inventory

evidence.name: Vendor inventory with owner, data and criticality
evidence.what: Vendor inventory
evidence.where: Vendors module.
evidence.shows: Each vendor with owner, service, data shared and criticality tier.

description: Vendors inherit the data entrusted to you, and their weaknesses become yours. Diligence scaled to risk is what makes that inheritance a decision rather than an accident.
implementation_guidance:
Assess vendor security before granting access to systems or data, with depth set by the vendor's criticality, and agree the terms its contract must carry, such as incident notice, audit rights, the security and service levels expected, limits on subcontracting and return or deletion of data at exit.
Obtain current independent assurance for critical vendors, such as a SOC 2 Type II report, an ISO/IEC 27001 certificate with its Statement of Applicability, or a PCI DSS Attestation of Compliance where card data is involved, and read its scope, any exceptions or exclusions, the controls the vendor expects you to operate and the subservice providers it relies on, rather than filing it unread.
Re-review critical vendors at least annually and on material change, such as a breach, a change of ownership or a new subservice provider, including whether they met the security and service levels agreed in the contract.
Record the assessment, the agreed contract terms, the decision and any accepted risk. For suppliers that build software for you, also set security requirements and code ownership in the contract and test what they deliver before it goes live, and where a critical system depends on a supplier's code, such as core banking software, arrange source code escrow and verify the deposit is complete and current at each review.
name: Vendor security due diligence

description: Software adopted outside procurement still processes company data, but without a vendor review, a data processing agreement or an offboarding path. Detection is what brings it back under management.
implementation_guidance:
Monitor identity-provider sign-ins and OAuth grants to detect newly adopted applications.
Review expense and card data for software purchases made outside procurement.
Route detected applications into the vendor onboarding process, or remove access.
Make the approved request path easy enough that informal adoption is not the path of least resistance.
name: Shadow-IT detection

description: Subprocessors receiving customer or personal data extend the trust boundary. Customer contracts and privacy regimes commonly require that they are disclosed and, in many cases, that customers are notified before new ones are added.
implementation_guidance:
Maintain a subprocessor list recording the entity, purpose, data categories and location.
Publish it where customer commitments require, and keep the published version current.
Reconcile the list against vendors that actually receive data, using the data map.
Follow the contractual notice process before adding a subprocessor.
name: Subprocessor management

description: Where infrastructure runs in a cloud provider, physical security is performed by that provider and inherited rather than operated by you. Reviewing their independent assurance is what makes that reliance a verified control rather than an assumption.
implementation_guidance:
Obtain the provider's current independent assurance at least annually, such as a SOC 2 Type II report, an ISO/IEC 27001 certificate with its Statement of Applicability, or a PCI DSS Attestation of Compliance where card data is involved, and confirm it covers the regions and services you use.
Review any exceptions or exclusions and the controls the provider expects of you, such as complementary user entity controls or a shared responsibility matrix, and confirm you operate them.
Document the reliance, and which controls the provider operates, in your scope documents, such as the SOC 2 system description, the ISO/IEC 27001 Statement of Applicability or the PCI DSS service provider responsibility matrix.
Record the review, the reviewer and any issues identified.
name: Cloud physical security (provider assurance review)

description: Offices still hold laptops, printed material and network access. Where an office is in scope, physical access control is what stops digital controls from being bypassed by simply walking in.
implementation_guidance:
Control entry to offices and to any server room, data center or recovery site you run with badge or equivalent access, restrict server and network areas further, receive deliveries at a controlled point away from them, and keep those areas and screens showing sensitive work out of public view.
Keep a visitor log, escort visitors in secure areas, and set written rules for secure areas, such as no unsupervised visitors or contractors and no photography or recording without approval.
Detect unauthorized entry with intruder alarms or cameras that alert a named responder or monitoring service, or record the monitoring the building provides, and review alarm events, access exceptions and active badges against active staff at least quarterly.
Revoke badges at offboarding, retain access records and any footage for a defined period of at least 90 days where the law allows, secure printed confidential material and its disposal, and check desks, printers and secure areas on a quarterly walk-through.
